newsitem.title: USA: Experts foresee slightly wider U.S. May trade gap.
newsitem.headline: Experts foresee slightly wider U.S. May trade gap.

text.p: A further slowdown from the breakneck pace of first quarter export growth and another solid rise in imports should nudge the U.S. trade deficit higher for a second consecutive month in May, economists said this week.

Despite strong growth in the major trading partners of the United States, such as Canada and Mexico, experts surveyed by Reuters are calling for a modest uptick in the trade gap to $9.18 billion from $8.36 billion in April.
Among the reasons cited were a levelling off in robust aircraft exports and relative stability in oil prices, which declined substantially during the first few months of the year.
"Tumbling oil prices have meant that oil imports have been tumbling in nominal terms and aircraft exports have been stunning this year," said Christopher Low, senior economist at HSBC Markets Inc.

"For May it looks as though aircraft exports will be flat and oil prices were close to stable which means the underlying trend can shine through and I think it's pretty clear that there's a gradually rising deficit."

Low is calling for a shortfall of roughly $9.0 billion in May, with exports flat and imports up 1.0 percent. In April exports edged up by 0.2 percent to a record $78.36 billion, while imports climbed 0.9 percent to $86.72 billion -- also an historic high.
The rise in exports in April followed a whopping 5.1 percent advance in that sector during March, a trend which economists said could reverse, at least temporarily, in the May data.

"We think exports will be the big swing factor in this report," said William Dudley, chief U.S. economist at Goldman Sachs & Co, who is calling for a gap of $9.7 billion. "They were really strong in March and April but you could see a pretty big drop in May."
On a bilateral basis, Dudley said he expects improvement in the balances with NAFTA neighbors Canada and Mexico, which have both enjoyed robust growth.

In the April report, the Commerce Department reported that the trade deficit with Canada -- the country with which the United States has the largest volume of trade -- totalled $970 million, the lowest since March of 1995.
And department economist Lee Price said after the release of last month's report that the export trend with Mexico and Canada was "promising."
Most economists were calling for a widening in the trade gap with Japan, calling dollar strength against the yen a mild negative for the politically sensitive bilateral balance.

"I don't think that our problem in exporting to Japan is a currency problem but I do think that Japanese exporters have taken advantage of the recent strength of the dollar against the yen to step up market share, particularly in the automotive area," said Richard Berner, chief economist at Mellon Bank in Pittsburgh.

Economists played down the importance of Japan's June trade figures, released on Thursday, in predicting the U.S. bilateral figures for May. Japan reported that its overall trade surplus rose 27.7 percent year-over-year to 934.21 billion yen, and that its surplus with the U.S. climbed 26.8 percent to 373.14 billion yen
Berner said the trade gap with China should also broaden, but predicted strength in exports to Latin America and Europe.

He expects a narrower trade gap in May due to improving overseas growth and softness in imports as companies, which had built up inventories from imported sources, reduce their rate of inventory accumulation.
The Commerce Department will release its May report on international trade at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT on Friday, July 18.
